definition: A speculative decoding framework that adds multiple lightweight decoding heads to an LLM to predict several future tokens at once, which are then verified in parallel by the base model.
details: Medusa heads predict the token at offsets 1 through k, forming candidate continuations that are pruned with tree attention and verified in a single forward pass. The method requires no separate draft model and can be trained on a frozen backbone. Typical gains are 2–3x speedup over standard autoregressive decoding.

explainer.lead: Medusa speeds up generation by adding a few extra prediction heads to a model, each guessing a token further ahead, and checking the guesses in one pass. It matters because it gets speculative-decoding speedups without a separate draft model.

tiers.eli5: Picture a writer with several helpers, each shouting a guess for the second, third and fourth word ahead. The writer checks all the guesses at once and keeps the run that is right.
tiers.practitioner: Medusa heads sit on the last hidden state and predict tokens at offsets 1..k; their top choices form a candidate tree that tree attention verifies in a single forward pass. Medusa-1 trains only the heads on a frozen model, while Medusa-2 fine-tunes model and heads together for higher acceptance.
tiers.paperLevel: Cai et al. combine multiple decoding heads with tree-based attention over candidate continuations, and propose typical acceptance as a cheaper alternative to rejection sampling. This yields roughly 2-3x faster decoding, with Medusa-1 keeping the base model's outputs and Medusa-2 trading some fidelity for speed.

explainer.example: A chat assistant with four Medusa heads often accepts two or three tokens per forward pass instead of one.

citation.title: Medusa: Simple LLM Inference Acceleration Framework with Multiple Decoding Heads
